content:
Quick answer: Build your weekly shop around a varied, balanced diet: vegetables, fruit, beans, lentils, whole grains, unsalted nuts and unsaturated oils. Food choices support general health, but no individual food is a proven cure for arthritis.

How to use this shopping list

This guide is for planning affordable meals in UK supermarkets. If you have food allergies, kidney disease, diabetes, swallowing difficulties or another condition requiring a special diet, ask your clinician or registered dietitian for tailored advice.

Vegetables and fruit

  • Frozen mixed vegetables, spinach, broccoli, carrots and peppers
  • Apples, oranges, berries and bananas; frozen fruit is useful when fresh produce is expensive
  • Tinned tomatoes and vegetables without added salt where possible

Choose a variety rather than paying extra for products marketed as “anti-inflammatory”.

Whole grains and starchy foods

  • Porridge oats, brown rice, wholemeal bread and wholewheat pasta
  • Potatoes and other affordable starchy foods

Check packaging if you need gluten-free options or have other dietary restrictions.

Protein and dairy alternatives

  • Beans, chickpeas, lentils and tofu
  • Eggs, fish and lean meat if included in your diet
  • Plain yoghurt, milk or fortified alternatives suitable for your needs

Choose protein sources that suit your budget, beliefs and medical needs. Do not change prescribed medication because of dietary claims.

Oils, nuts and practical extras

  • Olive or rapeseed oil for everyday cooking
  • Unsalted nuts or seeds if safe for you
  • Herbs, spices, lemon and garlic for flavour instead of relying on salt

Turmeric and ginger can be used as food ingredients. Supplements may interact with medicines and should not be treated as replacements for medical care.

A simple week of meals

Breakfast: porridge with fruit. Lunch: lentil soup and wholemeal toast. Dinner: vegetables with beans, fish or tofu and rice. Vary portions and ingredients according to your appetite, nutrition needs and preferences.

What does the evidence say?

The NHS Eatwell Guide supports a varied balanced eating pattern for general health. NICE guidance for osteoarthritis emphasises therapeutic exercise and weight management where appropriate; it does not recommend a particular food as a cure. Claims that a specific diet will reverse joint damage should be treated cautiously.

When to seek advice

If joint symptoms are new, persistent or worsening, seek medical assessment rather than relying on diet alone. A suddenly hot, swollen joint with fever or feeling unwell needs urgent medical assessment because infection is possible.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: The Eatwell Guide
  • NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s
